ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Vascular Surgery Referral — Albert Einstein

code.originalText: Establishing care for a known abdominal aortic aneurysm: duplex ultrasound, blood pressure, lipids, smoking, and emergency symptoms

text.paragraph: Infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm of 5.0 cm by duplex ultrasound in a 70-year-old man, found at an exploratory laparotomy for abdominal pain and wrapped rather than repaired. Please advise on surveillance, the thresholds and options for elective repair, and medical therapy, and record a shared decision with him. [S]
Urgency: Routine, within four weeks, on the same day as his CT angiography results visit. [S]

list.item: Does the CT angiography confirm an aneurysm below the repair threshold, and does the old wrapping change his risk or the plan?
How often, and by which test, should the aneurysm be measured?
At what diameter, growth rate, or symptoms would you advise elective repair, and is his anatomy suitable for endovascular repair?
What medical therapy do you advise: blood pressure target, statin, and antiplatelet therapy?
Should other arteries be checked for aneurysms?
Please record a shared decision with him about repair, including his preferences.

text.paragraph: Episodes of severe abdominal pain led to an exploratory laparotomy, at which an abdominal aortic aneurysm was found; it could not be removed, and its front was wrapped to provoke scarring. He has had no abdominal pain since. Duplex ultrasound today: infrarenal aorta 5.0 cm. CT angiography ordered for anatomy. Pipe smoker since his youth, about five or six bowls a day; quit date set for next week with a 14 mg nicotine patch and 2 mg lozenges. Hypertension on amlodipine 5 mg, 146/86 mmHg today; losartan 50 mg added. Atorvastatin 40 mg started; LDL 142 mg/dL. Creatinine 1.02 mg/dL, eGFR 77, potassium 4.3, HbA1c 5.6 percent, urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio 14 mg/g, hemoglobin 14.2 g/dL, platelets 232. No diabetes, angina, stroke, or claudication. Independent, works most days, walks an hour a day. Weight 79 kg, BMI 26.7. No known allergy [S]

list.item: An abdominal operation for episodes of abdominal pain found a large swelling of the main artery in his abdomen, which was wrapped rather than repaired; he wants to know its size, how it will be watched, and when an operation would be advised. [S]
He has smoked a pipe since his youth and is willing to try to stop. [S]
His blood pressure has stayed above target on one medicine. [S]

text.paragraph: Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Albert Einstein was born on March 14, 1879, in Ulm, in the Kingdom of Wurttemberg, German Empire. [D]
He worked at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton from 1933 until his death and became a United States citizen in 1940. [D]
At about 69 he began to have intermittent episodes of severe abdominal pain, at times bad enough to make him vomit, which grew worse toward the end of 1948. [D]

On December 31, 1948, at the Jewish Hospital of Brooklyn, the surgeon Rudolph Nissen performed an exploratory laparotomy and found an abdominal aortic aneurysm described as the size of a grapefruit; because it could not be removed with the surgery of the time, he wrapped its front in cellophane to provoke scarring that might prevent growth and rupture. [D]
He recovered slowly and left the hospital about three weeks after the operation. [D]
Einstein was a long-time pipe smoker; a pipe was characteristic of his appearance, and an account of his aneurysm says he had smoked constantly since adolescence. [D]
Retrospective writers have suggested that he had features of the autism spectrum. [R]

list.item: Infrarenal abdominal aortic aneurysm, 5.0 cm by duplex ultrasound, found and wrapped at a prior exploratory laparotomy; under surveillance below the repair threshold: active, confirmed [S]
Essential hypertension: active, confirmed [S]
Nicotine dependence, pipe tobacco: active, confirmed [S]

Aneurysm imaging: duplex ultrasound today and CT angiography within two weeks for baseline anatomy; then duplex ultrasound every six months while the diameter is 5.0 to 5.4 cm, with CT if ultrasound views are poor. Guideline: The Society for Vascular Surgery practice guidelines on the care of patients with an abdominal aortic aneurysm (2018); 2022 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Aortic Disease (2022) [S]

Blood pressure below 130/80: add losartan 50 mg to amlodipine, home blood pressure readings twice daily for a week before each visit, and a metabolic panel two to four weeks after each change, then every six months. Guideline: 2022 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Aortic Disease (2022); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, Hypertension and Hyperlipidemia monographs (2026) [S]

Atorvastatin 40 mg each evening, with a baseline ALT and a lipid panel four to twelve weeks after starting, then yearly. Guideline: The Society for Vascular Surgery practice guidelines on the care of patients with an abdominal aortic aneurysm (2018); 2022 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Aortic Disease (2022); CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, Hypertension and Hyperlipidemia monographs (2026) [S]

Tobacco cessation: the 5 A's at every visit, a quit date within a week, a 14 mg nicotine patch with 2 mg lozenges for cravings, stepping down over the following months, and the state quitline. Guideline: The Society for Vascular Surgery practice guidelines on the care of patients with an abdominal aortic aneurysm (2018); 2022 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Aortic Disease (2022); Tobacco Smoking Cessation in Adults, Including Pregnant Persons: Interventions (2021) [S]

Emergency plan: sudden severe abdominal, back, flank, or groin pain, fainting, or a tender pulsating lump means calling emergency services at once; carry an aneurysm wallet card; avoid fluoroquinolone antibiotics unless there is no alternative. Guideline: The Society for Vascular Surgery practice guidelines on the care of patients with an abdominal aortic aneurysm (2018); 2022 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Aortic Disease (2022) [S]

Monitor on the CMID hypertension and hyperlipidemia schedules: blood pressure and weight at every visit; metabolic panel every six months on losartan; lipids, HbA1c, and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio yearly; baseline ECG; eye examination yearly; ankle-brachial index every two to three years. Guideline: CMID: Clinical Monitoring Intelligence Database, Hypertension and Hyperlipidemia monographs (2026) [S]
